title: Night shift at the bakery
topic: a student's summer job in a bakery

paragraphs.text: His lessons were rarely direct. He would never say 'knead the dough for longer'. Instead, he would take my hand and press it into the mixture so that I could feel the difference between dough that was ready and dough that was not. 'Bread is not a recipe,' he liked to say. 'It is a conversation.' Slowly, my hands began to understand what my head could not.

Mr Ferraro was back behind the counter within a week, a little thinner and under strict instructions from his doctor to work fewer hours. When his daughter told him what had happened, he said nothing. But the next morning, I found a new apron hanging on my hook, with my name stitched onto the pocket.

That confidence lasted until my first shift, which began at half past two in the morning. When I arrived, the street outside was completely dark and silent, but the bakery was already full of light and noise. Mr Ferraro, the owner, handed me an apron without a word and pointed at a mountain of flour sacks that needed carrying down to the cellar.

Looking back, I am not sure why I applied for the job at all. My friends had found work in shops and restaurants, with normal hours and the chance to spend their evenings together, and several of them offered to put in a good word for me. I turned them all down, and for most of the summer I barely saw them.

I asked her to give me one night first. I am still not entirely sure where the idea came from, but I found myself promising that the regular customers would have their bread as usual, and that I would phone her if anything went wrong. She hesitated, then agreed, probably because she was too worried about her father to argue.

Mr Ferraro's reaction to the fire surprised me. Instead of shouting, he calmly put it out with a damp cloth, looked at me for a long moment and then burst out laughing. 'In forty years,' he said, 'I have burnt more bread than you will ever see. Now you are a real baker.' It was the first time he had said more than a dozen words to me.

Not everything went smoothly, of course. The oven had a temper of its own, and on humid days the dough refused to rise no matter what we did. But I had begun to look forward to my shifts, which I would never have predicted in June. I even started to enjoy the walk to work through the empty streets, when the only other people awake seemed to be the delivery drivers and the birds.

items.hint: The paragraph before ends with the writer feeling sure that early mornings would be easy. Which paragraph shows that feeling did not last?
items.explanation: C begins 'That confidence lasted until my first shift', referring back to the writer's belief that early mornings 'could not be that bad', and introduces Mr Ferraro before he is mentioned by name later.

items.hint: The previous paragraph ends with a tea towel catching fire.
items.explanation: F describes 'Mr Ferraro's reaction to the fire', and his first real conversation with the writer leads to 'From then on, he began to talk while we worked'.

items.hint: The paragraph before ends 'he was teaching me'. How did he teach?
items.explanation: A explains that 'His lessons were rarely direct', developing the idea that his stories were a form of teaching.

items.hint: The next paragraph begins 'Then, in the last week of the summer…'. Which paragraph describes the weeks before that?
items.explanation: G sums up how the job had gone ('Not everything went smoothly') and how the writer now enjoyed it, before the sudden change introduced by 'Then'.

items.hint: The daughter says the shop will have to close. How does the writer respond?
items.explanation: In E the writer asks her 'to give me one night first', which leads directly to 'That night was the longest of my life'.

items.hint: What happened when Mr Ferraro came back?
items.explanation: B tells us Mr Ferraro returned and rewarded the writer with an apron, which closes the story before the writer's final reflection. D does not fit anywhere: the first paragraph already explains why the writer applied.

title: A website for the shop
topic: helping a family business to go online

paragraphs.text: He also started making suggestions, some of them excellent. It was his idea to add a short video of him demonstrating how to sharpen a kitchen knife, which has now been watched more often than anything else on the site. Several viewers have written to ask whether he gives lessons. He is considering it.

Within a few days of the launch, orders were arriving from all over the country, and we had to take on a part-time assistant to deal with them. My uncle, delighted, began talking about opening a second shop in the city centre, and I started to wonder whether I needed to finish my degree at all.

That condition proved impossible to respect. Before I could put a single product online, I needed to know what the shop actually had, and the only complete record of the stock existed inside my uncle's head. So I spent three weeks counting, photographing and labelling, while he followed me around complaining that I was moving things.

As for me, the project ended up as the subject of my final-year dissertation, which my tutor described as 'refreshingly practical'. I am not sure my uncle has read it. He did, however, frame the first online order and hang it behind the counter, next to a photograph of the shop on its opening day.

I was, I suppose, the obvious choice. I was studying business, I spent most of my life online, and I had once built a website for a school project that received a respectable grade. What nobody at the table seemed to realise was that selling ten thousand different products online is rather more complicated than designing a page about the solar system.

So we changed our strategy. Instead of trying to list everything, we concentrated on the unusual items: spare parts for old appliances, traditional tools, the odd sizes of screws that modern furniture no longer uses. I wrote short articles explaining how to repair things, and people began to find the shop through search engines while looking for solutions to their problems.

We launched the site on a Monday in October. My uncle insisted on printing the home page and sticking it to the shop window, which I thought rather missed the point, and I sent a message to every customer whose email address he had. There were eleven of them, three of whom were relatives.

items.hint: Everyone at the table turns to look at the writer. Why?
items.explanation: E explains why the writer was 'the obvious choice' to build the website, which is why everyone turned to look at them.

items.hint: The uncle's condition was that nothing in the shop should change.
items.explanation: C begins 'That condition proved impossible to respect', referring to the uncle's demand that the writer should not 'change anything'.

items.hint: The next paragraph starts 'Not one of them placed an order.' Who are 'them'?
items.explanation: G ends with the eleven customers who received an email about the launch; 'Not one of them' refers to these eleven people.

items.hint: The writer realises the shop can win with things the chain does not sell. What do they do next?
items.explanation: F begins 'So we changed our strategy' and describes focusing on unusual items, which explains the growth in online sales 'By Christmas'.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'That video'. Which paragraph introduces a video?
items.explanation: A continues the description of the uncle's new attitude ('He also started making suggestions') and introduces the knife-sharpening video that 'That video' refers to.

items.hint: The final paragraph mentions 'My tutor's description'.
items.explanation: D mentions the dissertation that the writer's tutor described as 'refreshingly practical', which the last paragraph refers back to. B does not fit: it contradicts the slow start and the modest results described in the text.

title: The mountain that taught me patience
topic: a first attempt at climbing a mountain

paragraphs.text: The descent was slow and humbling. I walked down through the cloud with my eyes fixed on the stones that marked the path, counting them under my breath, and it was nearly dark when the lights of the hut appeared below me. My grandfather was sitting outside, wrapped in a blanket, as if he had known all along exactly when I would arrive.

My grandfather clearly disagreed. He looked at my brand-new boots, my enormous rucksack and the chocolate bars I had packed instead of proper food, and shook his head. 'The mountain does not care how much you have read,' he said. Then he insisted on coming with me as far as the first hut, which, at seventy-eight, he reached long before I did.

Just as I was about to give up, the cloud lifted as suddenly as it had arrived, and I reached the summit with the whole valley spread out beneath me. I remember thinking that it had been worth every step, and I took a photograph to show my grandfather as proof.

It took me a long time to believe him. For weeks afterwards, I felt that I had failed, and I avoided looking at the mountain from the kitchen window. Friends who heard the story were kind but clearly puzzled: why would anyone walk for nine hours and then come home without reaching the summit?

The problem was not my legs but my pace. Eager to make up for lost time, I had been walking far too fast, stopping every twenty minutes to recover, then rushing on again. An older couple I met on the path walked steadily, without ever seeming to hurry, and yet they disappeared over the next ridge while I was still sitting on a rock, out of breath.

I have thought about that moment many times since, usually when I am impatient for something to happen at university or at work. Reaching a goal, it seems to me now, matters far less than knowing when to wait for a better day.

My progress, however, did not last. Shortly after two o'clock, the cloud that had been sitting harmlessly on the neighbouring peaks began to drift towards me, and within half an hour I could barely see the path in front of me. The guidebook had a single sentence about this situation: in poor visibility, do not continue.

items.hint: The writer believed they were 'thoroughly prepared'. Who thought otherwise?
items.explanation: B begins 'My grandfather clearly disagreed', contradicting the writer's belief, and mentions the first hut, which explains 'Above the hut, I continued alone'.

items.hint: By midday the writer had covered only half the distance. Why?
items.explanation: E explains that 'The problem was not my legs but my pace' and introduces the older couple, who are mentioned again later.

items.hint: The next paragraph mentions 'that advice'. Which paragraph contains advice?
items.explanation: G ends with the guidebook's advice not to continue in poor visibility, which the next paragraph refers to as 'that advice'.

items.hint: The writer has decided to turn back. What happens next, and where is the grandfather?
items.explanation: A describes the descent and the grandfather waiting at the hut, so 'He did not ask whether I had reached the top' follows naturally.

items.hint: The grandfather says the writer did well to turn back. Did the writer agree?
items.explanation: D begins 'It took me a long time to believe him', reacting to the grandfather's comment.

items.hint: The previous paragraph ends with 'the moment in the cloud'.
items.explanation: F refers to 'that moment' and reflects on it, before the final paragraph about the grandfather's notebook. C does not fit: the writer turned back on the first attempt and did not reach the summit.

title: A year out
topic: gap years between school and university
intro: Five people describe the year they took off between school and university.

sections.heading: Hannah – volunteering in a national park
sections.text: I spent nine months as a volunteer in a national park in northern Canada, clearing paths, counting birds and repairing fences. The work was physically exhausting, but I loved being outdoors all day and seeing the results of what I had done. What I had not anticipated was the isolation. The nearest town was three hours away by road, and for weeks at a time I saw nobody except the four other volunteers. In the first month, I phoned home almost every night. Gradually, though, I came to value the silence, and I read more books that winter than in the rest of my life put together. The biggest change was in my plans. I had a place to study law, but by the spring I knew I wanted to work with the natural world, so I reapplied for environmental science instead.

sections.heading: Omar – working at home
sections.text: My gap year was not glamorous. I worked full-time in the supermarket where I had had a Saturday job since I was sixteen, stacking shelves, working on the tills and, eventually, supervising the night shift. My parents were not impressed at first; they thought I was wasting a year that could have been spent studying, and my father reminded me of this regularly. But I had a plan. By living at home and spending almost nothing, I saved enough to pay my rent for the whole of my first year at university. That meant I could concentrate on my studies instead of working evenings like many of my friends. I also learnt how to deal with difficult customers, which has turned out to be surprisingly useful in group projects.

sections.heading: Julia – learning Japanese in Osaka
sections.text: I had studied Japanese at school for three years, so I arrived in Osaka feeling fairly confident. That confidence lasted about a day. People spoke so quickly, and used so much local dialect, that I understood almost nothing, and for the first couple of months I wondered whether I had made a terrible mistake. What saved me was the family I lived with. They spoke to me patiently, corrected my mistakes without making me feel stupid and included me in everything, from weekend trips to the grandmother's birthday party. By the time I left, I could hold a proper conversation, and I had a second family on the other side of the world. I am now studying Japanese and economics, and I go back to visit them every summer.

sections.heading: Tom – travelling in South America
sections.text: I travelled around South America for six months with a backpack and a budget of about fifteen euros a day. That meant sleeping in hostel dormitories, travelling on overnight buses and eating a great deal of rice. It was the best time of my life, but it was not always easy. In Bolivia, I left my bag unattended for a few minutes at a bus station and lost my passport, my bank card and most of my clothes. Sorting everything out took two weeks and taught me never to let my valuables out of my sight again. People sometimes assume that a year like mine is just a long holiday. In fact, organising every journey and every bed myself made me far more independent than I had been at school.

sections.heading: Lucía – working for a start-up
sections.text: I spent my gap year working for a small technology start-up in Barcelona. It sounded exciting, and in some ways it was. Because the company was so small, I was put in charge of its social media accounts within a week, even though I had no training and very little idea what I was doing. I learnt a lot, mostly by making mistakes in public. Looking back, though, I am not sure it was the best choice. I spent almost all my time in front of a screen, much as I would at university, and I sometimes envy friends who travelled or worked with their hands. If I could do it again, I would choose something that took me further out of my comfort zone.

items.statement: I travelled with a strict limit on how much I could spend each day.
items.hint: Who mentions a daily budget?
items.explanation: Tom travelled 'with a budget of about fifteen euros a day'. Omar spent very little too, but he stayed at home and did not travel.

items.statement: My family had doubts about the way I chose to spend the year.

items.explanation: Omar's parents thought he was 'wasting a year', and his father reminded him of it regularly.

items.explanation: Hannah did not anticipate 'the isolation' and phoned home almost every night in the first month.

title: Sharing a flat
intro: Five university students describe what it is like to share a flat.

sections.heading: Ben
sections.text: There are six of us in a rather tired old house near the station, and for the first term the kitchen was a disaster. We drew up a cleaning rota and stuck it on the fridge, but within a fortnight nobody was following it. Some people did more than their share and resented it; others genuinely did not seem to notice the dirty plates piling up. The atmosphere got quite tense. In the end, one of my flatmates suggested that we all put in a few euros a week and pay someone to clean the shared areas once a fortnight. It costs us less than a coffee each, and the arguments stopped almost overnight. Apart from that, we get on well, although six people sharing one bathroom will never be entirely peaceful.

sections.heading: Sofia
sections.text: I found my flat through a website for students, so I moved in with four complete strangers. I was nervous; I had heard plenty of horror stories about difficult flatmates. As it turned out, I was lucky. We are all studying different subjects, which means we have plenty to talk about and never compete with each other. Early on, someone suggested a film night every Thursday, and it has become something of a tradition: whoever chooses the film has to provide the snacks, and the debates afterwards often go on longer than the film itself. Two years later, the five of us are close friends, and we have already agreed to look for a bigger flat together next year.

sections.heading: Kwame
sections.text: When my best friend from school and I both got places at the same university, living together seemed like the obvious thing to do. It was a mistake. Little things that had never mattered before started to annoy us both: he left the heating on all day, and I never remembered to buy toilet paper. The real problems began with money. He earned more from his part-time job than I did, and he wanted to share the bills in a way I could not afford. We are still friends, but it took a long time to repair the damage, and we now live in separate flats. My advice to anyone in the same position is simple: keep your best friend as your best friend, and find someone else to live with.

sections.heading: Mei
sections.text: I am quite a quiet person, and I like to go to bed early, so I was a little worried when I discovered that two of my flatmates were enthusiastic party-goers. For the first few weeks, there was music in the living room until three in the morning at least twice a week. Rather than complain, I asked if we could sit down and talk about it. We agreed that weekday nights would be quiet after eleven, while weekends would be more relaxed. It has worked better than I expected, and they have been good about sticking to it. Even so, the flat is never completely silent, so I do most of my studying in the university library, which suits me anyway.

sections.heading: Pablo
sections.text: Most of my flatmates are undergraduates like me, but one of them, Chris, is in his thirties and finishing a doctorate after several years working as a chef. At first I assumed he would be the dull one. I could not have been more wrong. Before I met him, I lived mainly on pasta and frozen pizza; now I can make a proper risotto and a decent curry, because he spent several evenings patiently showing me how. Because he has already been through so much of what we are experiencing, he also gives sensible advice about exams, money and life after university, without ever lecturing us. Having someone a little older in the flat has made the whole experience calmer.

items.statement: I had never met my flatmates before moving in.
items.hint: Who moved in with 'complete strangers'?
items.explanation: Sofia found the flat through a website and moved in with four complete strangers.

items.statement: Living together damaged a friendship I already had.
items.hint: Who lived with a friend from school?
items.explanation: Kwame and his best friend fell out over money, and it took a long time to repair the damage.

items.hint: Who can now make risotto and curry?
items.explanation: Chris, a former chef, patiently showed Pablo how to cook.

items.statement: A system we introduced quickly broke down.

items.explanation: Ben's flat drew up a cleaning rota, but 'within a fortnight nobody was following it'.

items.hint: Who goes to the library?
items.explanation: Mei does most of her studying in the university library because the flat is never completely silent.

items.explanation: Sofia's flat has a film night every Thursday, which has become a tradition.

items.explanation: Kwame advises people to 'find someone else to live with' rather than their best friend.

items.hint: Who lives with someone in his thirties?
items.explanation: Pablo says having someone a little older in the flat has made the experience calmer and brought useful advice.

title: Earning while learning
topic: students with side jobs and small businesses
intro: Five students describe how they earn money alongside their studies.

sections.heading: Laura – handmade jewellery
sections.text: I started making earrings in my first year, purely for fun, using cheap beads and wire I bought online. Friends asked me to make pairs for them, then friends of friends, and eventually someone suggested I open an online shop. I now sell around forty pieces a month. I love the creative side: sitting at my desk in the evening with a podcast on, designing something new, is the most relaxing part of my week. What nobody warned me about was the administration. Once I was earning a regular income, I had to register as self-employed, keep records of every sale and every purchase, and fill in a tax return, which took me an entire weekend the first time. Still, the extra money means I no longer have to ask my parents for help with the rent.

sections.heading: Daniel – online tutoring
sections.text: Last year I worked in a café at weekends, which was tiring and paid badly. A friend suggested I try tutoring online instead, and I have never looked back. I help secondary school students prepare for their maths exams, mostly through video calls. Because I set my own timetable, I can fit lessons around lectures and simply take a week off when I have deadlines of my own. The pay is also far better: I earn roughly three times what I used to make for an hour of serving coffee. The best part, though, is the moment when a student who has been struggling suddenly understands something. Several parents have recommended me to others, so I now have more requests than I can accept.

sections.heading: Nina – dog walking
sections.text: I walk dogs for six families in my neighbourhood, usually two or three at a time, early in the morning and again in the late afternoon, at times that suit the owners rather than me. It is the perfect job for someone who hates sitting still: I walk at least fifteen kilometres a day, and I have never been fitter. The owners are an interesting mix of people, from a retired judge to a young couple who both work as nurses, and some of them have become friends. The main drawback is that the work is very uneven. In summer and at Christmas, when families go away and need someone to look after their dogs, I am busy every day; in February my earnings can fall by half. I have learnt to put money aside in the busy months.

sections.heading: Rafa – reselling trainers
sections.text: I study business, so when I noticed that certain limited-edition trainers were selling online for twice their original price, I saw an opportunity. I now buy and resell around twenty pairs a month, mainly through apps, though I also spend Saturday mornings at a second-hand market. It is not as easy as it sounds. Twice I have bought large numbers of a model that suddenly went out of fashion, and I had to sell them at a loss. Those mistakes taught me to research the market much more carefully before I spend anything. In fact, a lot of what I do – pricing, managing stock, keeping track of cash flow – is exactly what we study in my lectures, so I sometimes feel I am getting two educations at once.

sections.heading: Amira – transcription
sections.text: I transcribe interviews and podcasts for a couple of media companies, working from my room. In theory, it is ideal for a medical student. In practice, it is more complicated. Clients often send work with very short deadlines, and more than once I have stayed up all night to finish a transcription and then struggled to concentrate in a morning lecture. I have also found the work surprisingly lonely. Medicine is a sociable degree, but when I am transcribing I can spend six hours in my room with headphones on, speaking to nobody, and by the end of the day I am desperate for company. I am planning to look for something with more human contact next year.
